Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 65
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Retail Worker
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 60

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit, Distraction: I distract myself with something else, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time

Vignette:
The hurricane had turned his neighborhood into a churning river, and William remembered the moment the water breached his threshold and climbed the stairs with terrifying speed. He had scrambled to the second floor, but the front door jammed shut under the pressure, and the walls groaned as the foundation settled. For two days, he clung to the top of the staircase, listening to the house fracture around him, certain the structure would give way. When the rescue boat finally cut through the debris-choked windows, he felt no relief, only a raw, trembling exhaustion that had rewritten how he understood safety. The trapped darkness and structural collapse had rewired his sense of security, making the sound of rain or the sudden shift of a door feel like immediate threats rather than background noise. In the weeks that followed, William’s daily reality fractured into overlapping layers of memory and alertness. He had come to believe that the world was a dangerous place, where disaster could arrive without warning. He looked at his hands and felt they belonged to a man who had been fractured by the storm. He was certain that he had permanently changed for the worse, that he would never again be the steady presence his wife, Elena, relied on. What frightened him most was the thought that he had lost the ability to trust his own environment, so he resolved to stay perpetually on guard. These appraisals sat beside the memories that refused to fade into the past. When rain began to drum against his kitchen window, William would suddenly feel the cold seep up his legs, his breath catching as the staircase collapse played behind his eyes like a film running on repeat. He would blink, disoriented, certain the walls were groaning around him rather than the house settling in its sleep. The memory felt like it was happening right now, an unfolding present that demanded his full attention. These experiences occupied the same hours as his sleepless nights and his work schedule. He had come to believe he could not afford to rest. He found himself lying awake long after Elena had fallen into a deep, uninterrupted sleep, listening to the house for creaks, straining to catch the hum of a generator or the rush of a distant storm. He was always watching, always braced, his muscles coiled tight in a way that left him exhausted by morning. The need to monitor threat and the habit of staying near exits shaped his routine at the regional hardware store where he still worked the morning shift. As soon as he stepped through the employee entrance, his eyes darted to the rear doors, the service alley, and the loading dock. He made sure to stay near the nearest exit, positioning himself close to the stockroom corridor where he could see the street through the glass. Checking surroundings became a quiet habit; he timed his movements by the door frames and rarely wandered deep into the warehouse aisles. When a customer approached, or when the overhead PA system crackled with a delivery announcement, his attention would split. He learned to quickly shift his focus to inventory counts, distracting himself while his body remained locked in place. Over the months, these parallel habits accumulated consequences. He missed stocking cues, his supervisor noted his frequent near-miss with a falling pallet, and he began arriving late because he had spent twenty minutes circling the block to check drainage patterns around the store. Elena noticed the distance between them first; she would catch him staring at the front door during dinner, his fork hovering mid-air, his jaw tight, as if listening for a siren that wasn’t there. The overlapping pull of scanning the room and rehearsing exits left little space for conversation. The breaking point came three weeks ago when a summer thunderstorm knocked out power for twelve blocks. William had been in the store when the backup lights flickered on, and the sudden shift in pressure had triggered the film in his head so violently that he collapsed a display of extension cords, hyperventilating until a coworker called for help. He had left Elena alone with the groceries, hadn’t meant to make her watch him tremble in the parking lot as the rain poured over the awning. What terrified him now was not the storm itself, but the certainty that he was unraveling in real time, that his body had become a traitor that would never stop sounding the alarm. He had come to the clinic because he could no longer pretend the guardrails were holding. He hoped, quietly, that someone might help him remember how to walk through a room without already mapping the door, and that he might finally rest without feeling like he was surrendering to the dark.
